card_quote: What matters to her: accuracy and sources she can show students; age-appropriate stories; something that takes 5 minutes. / Constraints: school buys little; content must be safe for a classroom.
how_read: Cover to cover over about a week, mostly at my desk during planning periods, with sticky notes on the ones I could use as bell ringers. I read the history-ish rounds (1, 2, 7, 10) properly and skimmed the physics round and most of round 8, reading the question and the Tell someone line and moving on.

w1_friction.note: The copyright page still has a placeholder on it. Did anyone proof this before printing?
If I put this in front of kids, the first question will be whether a computer wrote it, and I won't have a good answer.
w1_friction.quote: the entries were drafted with AI tools

w1_best.why: Blood, toil, tears and sweat. Perfect five-minute opener, and it doubles as a lesson on the rule of three. Hansard as the source, which I can show them.
Habeas corpus and Magna Carta: my students all think the Constitution came straight out of 1215. Short, clean, and it connects to the Suspension Clause.
Eisenhower saying 'what you would call' the domino principle. That one detail is a great 'read the primary source closely' moment.
Rats with no tails. Kids would love it, and it pairs with the cobra one to show a documented case next to a legend.
Six downloads, two of them by her lawyers. They'd remember that number forever, and it's a nice way into why you shouldn't overreact online.

w1_flat.why: Contradicts itself and sits in the wrong round. The one American history story in that stretch and it's the broken page.
Unreadable. I couldn't tell you what it said without reading it twice.
Uncertainty principle. Fourier transforms lost me completely, and it's nowhere near anything I teach.
Maxwell's equations. Fine I suppose, but twenty equations versus four is not a story anyone in my building would care about.
Newton's apple again. It's the same story as the page before with the question turned around.

w1_review.headline: A handy bank of bell ringers, but check the Franklin page first
w1_review.body: I got a dozen solid five-minute openers out of this, especially the Churchill, habeas corpus and domino theory entries, and every answer lists where the claim comes from, which I can actually use to teach sourcing. The answers are written for adults, though, so with middle schoolers I'd only read the verdict and the last line. Two pages look like they were never checked: a Franklin kite entry that says TRUE and then says the opposite, and a goldfish page in impenetrable jargon, plus a missing ISBN. Bottom line: useful for teachers who pre-read, not a book to hand straight to students.

w2_review_first: I'd tell a colleague it's a quiz book of famous myths where you guess true, folklore or disputed, and a fair number work as warm-ups if you pre-read them. I'd also tell them it's more psychology and science than history, the answers are long for younger kids, and there's at least one page that contradicts itself, so don't trust it blind.

w2_lost.why: The physics round. Sinks, wings, quantum cats. I flipped through the questions and didn't read the answers.
Two Hanlon's razor entries back to back made me feel like I'd already read this page.
The goldfish page. I read two sentences, gave up and turned over.
Round 8 on software and management laws. Brooks, Conway, bike sheds. Not my world, not my students' world.

w2_read_aloud.why: The kids would all say 'blood, sweat and tears' and then find out they dropped a word. Instant hook.
Twain or Einstein and the answer is neither. Great for teaching that famous names get stuck on quotes.
For my older classes only. It's the textbook story they'll meet again, and it shows how one newspaper number spread.
Ties straight into the Constitution unit.
Cold War unit opener. The exact wording of the press conference is the whole lesson.

w2_cut.why: Says one thing in the verdict and another in the text. Either fix it properly or take it out.
Written in a completely different voice nobody can read, with no real source.
The word in the question means I can't use it in school, and the answer is just crud versus crap.
It's the Hanlon's razor story told a second time.
Too technical for a general reader and has nothing to do with folklore anyone repeats at dinner.

w2_book2: If the next one has another page where the stamp and the text disagree, I can't stand in front of thirty kids with it.
